items.title: Precepts in Detail: The Six Supports Restated, and What Success and Purity Look Like

items.zh: 不毀壞尸羅，於學誓能順，軌範無譏論，於五處遠離。若無犯、出離，無惡作、惡作，於彼學尋求，及勤修彼行。
items.en: Not violating one's moral discipline; keeping faithfully to one's vowed training; conduct beyond reproach; and staying clear of five particular places. Without transgression, and with release [should one lapse]; without remorse, and without [even the light offence of] wrongdoing; one seeks out this training, and diligently practises it.

items.zh: 終無有棄捨，命難亦無虧，常住正行中，隨毘柰耶轉。
items.en: Never abandoning it, suffering no diminishment even at the risk of one's life; ever abiding in right conduct, always acting in accordance with the discipline.

items.zh: 修治誓為先，亦修治淨命。二邊皆遠離，亦棄捨邪願。
items.en: Cultivating one's vow as the very first step; also cultivating a pure livelihood; keeping clear of both extremes; and abandoning any wrongly directed aspiration.

items.title: Precepts Complete: Diligence, Simplicity, and the Nine Marks of a True Renunciant

items.zh: 於諸障礙法，終無有耽染。亂心法纔生，尋當速遠離。非太沈、太浮，恒善住正念，根本眷屬淨，而修行梵行。
items.en: Towards whatever obstructs the training, one never grows attached or absorbed; the moment a disturbing state arises, one swiftly abandons it. Neither too submerged nor too exposed, ever well established in mindfulness — with both the root precepts and their auxiliary branches kept pure, one cultivates the holy life.

items.zh: 應發勤精進，常堅固勇猛。恒修不放逸，五支善安住。當隱自諸善，亦發露眾惡。得諸衣服等，麁、妙皆歡喜。少隨於世務，麁弊亦隨轉。受杜多功德，為寂離煩惱。
items.en: One should rouse diligent effort, ever firm and courageous, constantly practising heedfulness, well established in its five supports. One should hide one's own good qualities, yet openly disclose one's faults; whatever robes and the like one receives, coarse or fine, one should welcome with equal joy. Involving oneself little in worldly affairs, accepting whatever is plain and poor; undertaking the ascetic practices, for the sake of stillness and freedom from affliction.

items.zh: 當具足威儀，應量而攝受；終無有所為，詐現威儀相。不自說實德，亦不令他說。雖有所方求，而非現異相。從他邊乞求，終不強威逼；以法而獲得，得已、不輕毀。
items.en: One should fully maintain proper deportment, receiving only what is fitting in measure, never acting so as to falsely display an air of dignity in order to win gain. Not proclaiming one's own true virtues, nor letting others proclaim them; though one may indeed have some need, one does not display any strange or contrived appearance to attract notice. Seeking from another, one never coerces or intimidates; one obtains only through proper means, and having received it, never disparages the gift.

items.zh: 不耽著利養，及所有恭敬；亦不執諸見，增益與損減。不著順世間無義文呪術；亦不樂畜積無義長衣鉢。恐增諸煩惱，不染習居家；為淨修智慧，當親近賢聖。
items.en: Not craving gain, nor any degree of veneration; nor holding to any view, whether of over-imputation or under-imputation. Not attached to worldly ways, to pointless writings or incantations; nor delighting in hoarding superfluous robes or bowls. Fearing the increase of affliction, one does not grow habituated to household life; for the sake of purifying and cultivating wisdom, one draws near instead to the wise and the noble.

items.zh: 不畜朋友家，恐發憂悲、亂，能生苦煩惱；纔起、尋遠離。不受於信施，恐加害瘡皰；於如來正法，甞無有棄捨。於他愆犯中，無功用、安樂；常省自過失，知已、速發露。
items.en: Not keeping close ties with friends' households, fearing the sorrow and disturbance that follow, which give rise to suffering and affliction — the moment such attachment arises, one seeks at once to abandon it. Not accepting offerings given in faith carelessly, fearing to aggravate the wound they could become; towards the Tathāgata's true Dharma, one never abandons it. Amid others' faults and transgressions, one makes no effort [to seek them out], and dwells at ease; one constantly examines one's own faults, and upon recognising them, swiftly discloses them.

items.zh: 若犯於所犯；當如法出離。所應營事中，能勇勵自作。於佛及弟子、威德與言教，一切皆信受；觀大罪、不謗。於極甚深法，不可思度處，能捨舊師宗，不堅執自見。
items.en: If one transgresses in some way, one should rightfully find release from it; in whatever tasks are one's own responsibility, one applies oneself with courage and vigour. Towards the Buddha and his disciples — their majestic power and their teaching — one holds complete faith throughout, recognising that slander of them is a grave transgression, and refrains from it. Towards the most profound teaching, in that domain beyond ordinary thought and measure, one is able to relinquish one's former teachers' doctrines, and does not stubbornly cling to one's own views.

items.title: Concentration and Wisdom Complete: All Fifty-One Verses on the Three Trainings Close

items.zh: 常樂居遠離，及邊際臥具，恒修習善法，堅精進勇猛。無有欲、生欲、不憎惡、憎惡，離睡眠、睡眠，時不居寂靜，離惡作、惡作、無希慮、希慮，一切種恒時成就正方便。
items.en: Ever delighting in solitude, content with the plainest bedding and seat; constantly cultivating wholesome states, firm in courageous diligence. Without craving, generating the wish for the good; free of hostile aversion, yet averse to [one's own] hostility; free from torpor, keeping healthy rest; at the proper time, not remaining in stillness alone. Free from [the hindrance of] remorse, yet with the remorse that swiftly confesses wrongdoing; free from doubt, yet earnestly aspiring to the good to be attained — in every respect, at every moment, accomplishing right effort.

items.zh: 引發、與覺悟、及和合所結、有相、若親昵，亦多種喜樂、侵逼、極親昵，名虛妄分別。能生於欲貪，智者當遠離。諸欲、令無飽，眾多所共有，是非法因緣，能增長貪欲，賢聖所應離，速趣於壞滅，仗託於眾緣，危逸所依地。諸欲，如枯骨，亦如軟肉段，如草炬相似，猶如大火坑，譬如蟒毒蛇，亦如夢所見，如借莊嚴具，如樹端熟果。如是知諸欲，都不應耽樂。
items.en: Arousal, and awakening to it, and the bond formed through union; taking on a mark, growing intimate, and manifold delight; pressing closer still into utmost intimacy — these are called false conceptions, capable of giving rise to sensual craving; the wise should keep far from them. Sense-desires never satisfy; they are shared in common by many; they are the very cause of wrongdoing, and cause craving itself to grow. The noble ones rightly abandon them, for they rush swiftly towards ruin; resting only on a convergence of conditions, they are the very ground of ruinous heedlessness. Sense-desires are like a dry bone, like a piece of raw meat, like a torch of grass, like a great pit of fire; like a venomous serpent, like something seen only in a dream, like borrowed ornaments, like fruit ripening at a branch's very tip. Knowing sense-desires to be like this, one should never take delight in them.

items.zh: 當聽聞正法，常思惟；修習；先觀見麁靜；次於修一向，捨煩惱麁重，於斷生欣樂；於諸相觀察；得加行究竟；能離欲界欲，及離色界欲，入真諦現觀，能離一切欲，證現法涅槃，及餘依永盡。「
items.en: One should hear the true Dharma, constantly reflect on and cultivate it; first observe the coarse and the still, then apply oneself single-mindedly to cultivation, relinquishing affliction's coarse disturbance, taking joy in its cessation, examining every mark, until preparatory effort reaches its culmination. Able thus to leave behind desire for the sense-desire realm, and desire for the form realm, one enters direct realisation of the truths, able to leave behind desire altogether — realising nirvāṇa in this very life, and its final, remainderless end.

blocks.text: The rest of the fifty-one verses: first a long description of a renunciant's moral life, then shorter verses on concentration and on the wisdom that removes desire. These verses read almost like a rule of life for a monastic. For a lay reader, Jennafer included, they are a portrait of what pure conduct looks like from the inside.

Not violating moral discipline; keeping the vowed training (the prātimokṣa); conduct beyond reproach; avoiding five places unsuitable for a monastic (named in the prose, Day 135). Keeping them "even at the risk of one's life": Master Cháng Bǎi tells of a stream-enterer who would rather be killed than kill a sheep. Venerable Miào Jìng: this is the "firmness" of moral discipline.

subs.head: Pure livelihood and the middle way

blocks.text: "Pure livelihood": Venerable Miào Jìng puts it plainly: wealth not gained by improper means. One avoids the two extremes of indulgence and self-torment, and gives up wrongly directed aims such as wishing for rebirth in heaven.

"Neither too submerged nor too exposed": Venerable Miào Jìng: to commit a small fault, think nothing of it, and not confess it is to be "too submerged". The verses then paint the renunciant: diligent, hiding one's virtues and disclosing one's faults, content with coarse or fine robes alike, not seeking fame, not keeping close ties with lay households, not accepting faithful offerings carelessly.

Delight in solitude, simple bedding, constant wholesome practice. "Free from remorse, yet with remorse": Master Cháng Bǎi: the second "remorse" (惡作) means that when regret arises, one confesses quickly and is released.

The verses list the ways false conceptions give rise to sensual craving, then give eight similes for desires: a dry bone, a lump of raw meat, a grass torch, a pit of fire, a venomous snake, a dream, borrowed ornaments, ripe fruit at a tree's top. Master Cháng Bǎi matches each to a fault: like a dry bone, desire never satisfies; like raw meat, it is shared by many.

subs.head: The path to freedom from desire

blocks.text: Hearing, reflecting, cultivating; seeing the coarse and the calm; examining marks. Master Cháng Bǎi links this to the seven attentions (Day 108): at the stage of examining, coarse afflictions no longer appear, and one may think desire is gone; one deliberately calls up desire's attractive features to test whether one is really free. The verses end with entry into the truths and nirvāṇa in this life.

quiz.q: "No diminishment even at risk of life" shows the firmness of discipline. What story does Master Cháng Bǎi tell?
options: a stream-entrant boy who would rather die than kill a sheep — a stream-entrant's precepts are surely pure
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Because a stream-entrant's precepts are surely pure and he will not kill, he'd rather kill himself than the sheep." Venerable Miào Jìng: dying rather than breaking a precept is firmness.

quiz.q: Purity of discipline requires "a pure livelihood." What does Venerable Miào Jìng say pure livelihood is?
options: wealth not obtained unlawfully — that is pure livelihood
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Put plainly, if the wealth isn't from unlawful sources, that is called pure livelihood." One must also avoid the extremes of indulgence and self-torment and abandon wrong aims.

quiz.q: "Neither too submerged nor too exposed." What does Venerable Miào Jìng say "too submerged" is?
options: committing a small fault, not caring, and not confessing — that is "too submerged"
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "You commit a small fault, think nothing of it, and don't confess — that is called 'too submerged.'" "Too exposed" concerns obvious faults; the note's "excessive scruple" differs.

quiz.q: In "free from 惡作 [yet with] 惡作," what does the second 惡作 mean, per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: when there is regret, swiftly confessing and getting free, in accord with good — a positive sense
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "The second 惡作 means that when regret arises, one quickly confesses and is released, in accord with wholesome dharmas." The English treats it as something to remove.

quiz.q: Wisdom verses compare desires to a dry bone, raw meat, a grass torch, and so on. How does Master Cháng Bǎi relate the eight similes to the eight faults, and what does the note do?
options: they pair one by one with the eight faults — dry bone = never satisfying; raw meat = shared by many …; the note interprets them separately
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: desires are like a dry bone — never satisfying; like raw meat — anyone with money can have it, shared by many. Each simile matches one of the eight faults in order.

quiz.q: "Examining every mark, until preparatory effort culminates" — Master Cháng Bǎi links this to the attention of examination. What does it involve?
options: after a while coarse afflictions don't arise and one thinks desire is gone — one must evoke desirable images to test whether one is truly free
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: after a while coarse afflictions stop appearing and one thinks desire is gone — one must call up desire's attractive features and check whether one is free. The seven attentions are the lecture's mapping.
